- "supported": every factual part of the sentence (each number, each name, each count, each comparison, each cause, each "most", "all", "only" or "none") is stated by one or more of the claims, or follows from them directly with no new number. Give the ids of the claims that together support it.

- "no_factual_content": the sentence states nothing that could be true or false about the world: a transition, a statement of what the section will do, a definition of a word the report uses.

The NAMES table maps a code in a claim to the name a sentence uses; a sentence that uses the name is read as if it used the code. A sentence that names a statistical body is checked against the claims for that body.

Searches: manifest title scan and corpus text grep for 'Longpre', 'Consent in Crisis', 'crawler' (vendor documentation only: cloudflare-ai-crawl-control, rfc-9309, the OpenAI, Anthropic and Perplexity crawler pages); WebSearch 'study robots.txt AI crawlers blocked federal government .gov websites measurement GPTBot'; read Liu et al., 'Somesite I Used To Crawl' (IMC 2025, cseweb.ucsd.edu), which has no government category; read Ahrefs (above), category-level only.
    evidence: Longpre, S.; Mahari, R.; Lee, A.; et al. | 2024 | Consent in Crisis: The Rapid Decline of the AI Data Commons | abstract | quote: "in a single year (2023-2024) there has been a rapid crescendo of data restrictions" | note: An audit of 14,000 web domains behind C4, RefinedWeb and Dolma; robots.txt and terms of service, longitudinal.
    evidence: OpenAI, Overview of OpenAI crawlers, OAI-SearchBot row | quote: "opted out of OAI-SearchBot will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers"
    evidence: Anthropic support article on its crawlers, Claude-SearchBot row | quote: "may reduce your site's visibility and accuracy in user search results"
    evidence: Stox, P. | 2025 | The AI Bots That ~140 Million Websites Block the Most | body text beside the chart 'AI block rate over time by domain category' | quote: "law & government (42% blocked) sites blocked them more" | note: The nearest thing to a government-specific measure found: a category of about 140 million sites' robots.txt files, with no separation of U.S. federal .gov sites.

SENTENCES
S1: Turning from the record behind the framework to what the scanner itself observed, an access denial is the most direct observation, because it is the host's own answer to a plain, unauthenticated client that identified itself and obeyed robots.txt.
S2: Across all 1,055 findings, 341 are access denials, in which the host returned an HTTP 401, 403 or 429 status, disallowed the request in its robots.txt file, or reset the connection.
S3: The other findings comprise 415 absences, where the record, field or file is not served, 57 cases where something is served but fails the test applied to it, 65 other errors such as server errors, unparseable responses and a redirect loop, and 177 passes.
S4: Three statistical bodies account for the most complete refusals.
S5: The scanner met a denial on all 45 of its findings for the Bureau of Labor Statistics and on all 45 for the Office of Research, Evaluation, and Statistics at the Social Security Administration, so neither body produced a single absence or a single pass.
S6: The Bureau of Transportation Statistics came close behind, refusing the scanner on 41 of its 45 findings and passing only 2.
S7: Bodies with more findings were refused less completely but still often; for example, the Bureau of Economic Analysis denied the scanner on 40 of 89 findings, and the National Agricultural Statistics Service on 36 of 89.
S8: At the other end of the range, Statistics of Income at the Internal Revenue Service denied the scanner on only 4 of its 67 findings, all of them robots.txt disallows, although 44 of its findings are absences and only 12 pass.
S9: The National Center for Education Statistics and the National Animal Health Monitoring System each refused 10 of 45.
S10: Data.gov is a comparator host and not a statistical body, so it is reported apart from them; it refused 1 of its 9 findings and passed 7.
S11: These denials say something about public access as well as about the scanner, because the public's access through AI tools depends on the restrictions that publishers place on crawlers.
S12: OpenAI, for example, states that a site opted out of its search crawler will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers.
S13: A search of the literature found no earlier measurement of the AI-crawler policies of U.S. federal sites, and the nearest measure, taken across about 140 million websites, reports that law and government sites blocked AI bots more than other categories, with 42% blocked.
